An album, perhaps better defined as a "Long Play" (LP) release, generally consists of previously unreleased material (unless this type is combined with secondary types which change that, such as "Compilation").
An episodic release that was originally broadcast via radio, television, or the Internet, including podcasts.
Any release that does not fit or can't decisively be placed in any of the other categories.

A single has different definitions depending on the market it is released for.

  • In the US market, a single typically has one main song and possibly a handful of additional tracks or remixes of the main track; the single is usually named after its main song; the single is primarily released to get radio play and to promote release sales.
  • The U.K. market (also Australia and Europe) is similar to the US market, however singles are often released as a two disc set, with each disc sold separately. They also sometimes have a longer version of the single (often combining the tracks from the two disc version) which is very similar to the US style single, and this is referred to as a "maxi-single". (In some cases the maxi-single is longer than the release the single comes from!)
  • The Japanese market is much more single driven. The defining factor is typically the length of the single and the price it is sold at. Up until 1995 it was common that these singles would be released using a mini-cd format, which is basically a much smaller CD typically 8 cm in diameter. Around 1995 the 8cm single was phased out, and the standard 12cm CD single is more common now; generally re-releases of singles from pre-1995 will be released on the 12cm format, even if they were originally released on the 8cm format. Japanese singles often come with instrumental versions of the songs and also have maxi-singles like the UK with remixed versions of the songs. Sometimes a maxi-single will have more tracks than an EP but as it's all alternate versions of the same 2-3 songs it is still classified as a single.

There are other variations of the single called a "split single" where songs by two different artists are released on the one disc, typically vinyl.

An EP is a so-called "Extended Play" release and often contains the letters EP in the title. Generally an EP will be shorter than a full length release (an LP or "Long Play") and the tracks are usually exclusive to the EP, in other words the tracks don't come from a previously issued release. EP is fairly difficult to define; usually it should only be assumed that a release is an EP if the artist defines it as such.
A release mostly consisting of field recordings (such as nature sounds or city/industrial noise).
An audio drama is an audio-only performance of a play (often, but not always, meant for radio). Unlike audiobooks, it usually has multiple performers rather than a main narrator.
An audiobook is a book read by a narrator without music.

A compilation, for the purposes of the MusicBrainz database, covers the following types of releases:

  • a collection of recordings from various old sources (not necessarily released) combined together. For example a "best of", retrospective or rarities type release.
  • a various artists song collection, usually based on a general theme ("Songs for Lovers"), a particular time period ("Hits of 1998"), or some other kind of grouping ("Songs From the Movies", the "Café del Mar" series, etc).

The MusicBrainz project does not generally consider the following to be compilations:

  • a reissue of an album, even if it includes bonus tracks.
  • a tribute release containing covers of music by another artist.
  • a classical release containing new recordings of works by a classical artist.
  • a split release containing new music by several artists

Compilation should be used in addition to, not instead of, other types: for example, a various artists soundtrack using pre-released music should be marked as both a soundtrack and a compilation.
A promotional release mostly meant to have limited circulation and demonstrate the sound of an artist to record labels, publishers and other artists.

A DJ-mix is a sequence of several recordings played one after the other, each one modified so that they blend together into a continuous flow of music. A DJ-mix release requires that the recordings be modified in some manner, and the DJ who does this modification is usually (although not always) credited in a fairly prominent way.
An interview release contains an interview, generally with an artist.
A release that was recorded live. Generally this means "with an audience", be it in person, through the radio or in another similar way.

Promotional in nature (but not necessarily free), mixtapes and street albums are often released by artists to promote new artists, or upcoming studio albums by prominent artists. They are also sometimes used to keep fans' attention between studio releases and are most common in rap & hip hop genres. They are often not sanctioned by the artist's label, may lack proper sample or song clearances and vary widely in production and recording quality. While mixtapes are generally DJ-mixed, they are distinct from commercial DJ-mixes (which are usually deemed compilations) and are defined by having a significant proportion of new material, including original production or original vocals over top of other artists' instrumentals. They are distinct from demos in that they are designed for release directly to the public and fans; not to labels.
A release that primarily contains remixed material.

A soundtrack is the musical score to a movie, TV series, stage show, video game, or other medium. Video game CDs with audio tracks should be classified as soundtracks because the musical properties of the CDs are more interesting to MusicBrainz than their data properties.
German tape cartridge format, using grooved tape rather than magnetic tape.
Flexi-discs are phonograph records made of a thin, flexible vinyl sheet with a molded-in groove, designed to be playable on a normal phonograph turntable.
The CD layer of a DVDplus. The DVD layer should be added as a separate medium.
The DVD (audio) layer of a DVDplus. The CD layer should be added as a separate medium.
Video High Density (VHD) was a videodisc format which was marketed predominantly in Japan by JVC.
90 rpm, vertical-cut shellac discs, produced by the Pathé label from 1906 to 1932.

The Capacitance Electronic Disc (CED) is an analog video disc playback system developed by RCA, in which video and audio could be played back on a TV set using a special needle and high-density groove system similar to phonograph records.
The CD layer of a hybrid SACD. The SACD layer should be added as a separate medium.
The SACD layer of a hybrid SACD. The CD layer should be added as a separate medium.
The DVD (audio) layer of a DualDisc. The CD layer should be added as a separate medium.
The DVD (video) layer of a DualDisc. The CD layer should be added as a separate medium.
The CD layer of a DualDisc. The DVD layer should be added as a separate medium.
Shellac records were the most predominant type of gramophone record during the first half of the 20th century.
The DVD side of a vinyl + DVD VinylDisc. The vinyl side should be added as a separate medium.
The vinyl side of a VinylDisc. The CD or DVD side should be added as a separate medium.
The CD side of a vinyl + CD VinylDisc. The vinyl side should be added as a separate medium.
The DVD (video) layer of a DVDplus. The CD layer should be added as a separate medium.

A "digital collectible" device, mostly used for k-pop music, that is connected to a phone via Bluetooth or headphone jack and unlocks the release for listening in a companion app for a limited period of time.

A card (or other similar physical support) that doesn't contain the music itself directly, but provides a code to download it digitally. Often bundled with physical releases but sometimes sold as a standalone item (especially in Asia).
A very small optical disc in a protective case that was intended for portable listening. It did not find commercial success, but a few albums were released in the format in the early 00s.
A video format used in the 1980s and 90s for professional work, including television and video archival.

Copy Control CD (CCCD) is an umbrella term for CDs released circa 2001-2006 containing software that is ostensibly designed to prevent the CD from being ripped. There are a number of software variants: the most well-known are Macrovision's Cactus Data Shield (CDS) and SunnComm's MediaMax.
This represents the multichannel table of contents on a hybrid SACD's SACD layer.
This represents the multichannel table of contents on a SACD.
This represents the 2 channel (stereo/mono) table of contents on a SHM-SACD.
This represents the multichannel table of contents on a SHM-SACD.
This represents the 2 channel (stereo/mono) table of contents on a hybrid SACD's SACD layer.
This represents the 2 channel (stereo/mono) table of contents on a SACD.
A CD that contains both audio and data in the same session. The data is often in the first track, that will have to be skipped in many audio players. Relatively common in old video game CDs.

A CD that contains two sessions, one with audio and one with data. Since they are properly separated, audio players will not try to play the data session and it won't be part of the disc ID for the CD.
The DVD layer of a DualDisc, when it's unclear whether it should be DVD-Audio or DVD-Video (or it includes both). The CD layer should be added as a separate medium.
A standard size CD with the playing/data area of a 8cm CD; the remaining area is empty clear/translucent plastic, sometimes printed.
One-sided 3" vinyl records to be played with purpose-built players; originally developed in Japan and now mostly found as a Record Store Day curiosity.
A standard size DVD with the playing/data area of a 8cm MiniDVD; the remaining area is empty clear/translucent plastic, sometimes printed.
8cm DVD, often used for video singles.
Flat discs with grooves used in phonographs/gramophones. For shellac and vinyl records, use that specifically.
A CD format that combines data/video and audio, used for different purposes in the 1990s including, in some cases, music releases with accompanying video content.
A read only memory cartridge or card, such as the ones used by early home computers and some video game systems.
Enhanced version of Blu-ray supporting 4K Ultra HD video which is not compatible with all Blu-ray players.
